To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the kinetics of the heparan sulfates regrowth in the endothelial glycocalyx are dependent on the hemodynamic environment and are controlled by a differential in the endocytic and the exocytic membrane transport.
the heparin sulfate component of the endothelial cell glycocalyx increases by 1,4-fold following the application of high shear stress.

the heparin sulfate content of the glycocalx increases by 1,4-fold in response to laminar shear flow, with a time-constant of 19 h, while the cell alignment to the flow direction is maximal after 36 h.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of the glycocalix in the context of hemodynamics and its implications for the development of atherosclerotics.
the role of the glycocalix in endothelial cell adaptation to hemodynamic shear stress.
the dynamics of heparan sulfate in HUVECs exposed to high-shear stress, and the kinetics of glycocalyx formation following degradation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the endothelial cells’ ability to restore its glycocalyx layer following degradation is faster under high shear stress than in the absence of flow.
the heparin sulfate layer of endothelial cells regrows faster under flow than under static conditions.
the glycocalys is a highly dynamic structure, and the rate of its turnover is dependent on the hemodynamic conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the endothelial cells are able to adapt its glycocalyxlayer to a new hemodynamic environment in 24 h.
the glycocalxy of HUVEC cells under high-shear conditions is restored to a level of 1.4 times higher than the static cultured cells.
the endothelium is a dynamic system that can adapt its glycocalix to the local hemodynamic environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the glycocalys is an adaptive structure that is able to sense and adapt to changes in the local hemodynamic environment.
the endothelial glycocalyx is a dynamic structure that adapts to the local shear stress environment.
the glycocalys can be rapidly restored to the cell membrane in response to hemodynamic shear stress.
